rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.4 describe a greenhouse experiment (Araras, Brazil, Oct-Dec 2012) with two drip-irrigation treatments (T1 drinking water + full fertilization; T2 treated wastewater + partial fertilization), four plots each, two lettuce cycles. Q2: Section 3.3 and Table 6: fresh weight of lettuce under T2 (drip with TWW) was significantly larger than T1 (0.26 vs 0.18 kg/plant in cycle 1, 48% larger; 0.17 vs 0.08 in cycle 2, 100% larger); both treatments applied by drip at field capacity. Q4: Table 1 quantifies nutrient inputs in the irrigation water (TIN, P, K, Ca at least 200% higher in TWW), Fig. 3 reports daily soil-moisture monitoring with EnviroSCAN probes, Table 5 reports leaf nutrient concentrations and Table 6 root surface area, i.e. the intermediate nutrient/water-supply variables through which the yield effect is argued to arise (Section 3.3: T2 supplied nutrients during the whole cycle). Q8: Section 2.1 states the study was conducted with one repetition (two cycles); Conclusions recommend evaluating longer-cycle crops with more repetitions and field trials under the same conditions, i.e. limits of the greenhouse, single-crop, short-duration design. Q9: Table 6 reports MSD and CV% for fresh weight for each cycle (CV 16.40% and 29.14%).
rows.notes: The study compares treated wastewater versus drinking water, both applied by drip in a greenhouse; the yield difference is attributed to nutrient supply from the wastewater, not to the drip method itself, which is not isolated by any treatment. Q2 answered yes because the passage reproduces the study's own comparison (TSE drip with partial fertilization vs fresh water with conventional fertilization), but the evidence is about wastewater reuse under drip rather than about drip per se. Q3 no: fresh weight measured by a single method (harvest weighing). Q5/Q6 no: one soil (Dusky Red Latosol), one crop, one greenhouse, plot scale. Q7 no: the need to complement TWW nitrogen with fertilizer is a design choice/cited point, not stated as a requirement for the yield effect from own findings. Leaf nutrient concentrations did not differ between treatments, so the mechanism is only partly supported.

notes: Full text appears complete. Single-site greenhouse study, two cycles, one soil and one lettuce cultivar; all comparisons by ANOVA/Tukey with MSD and CV% reported.
